13777-the-siege-of-kimberley-its-humorou:
T. Phelan spent eighteen weeks inside Kimberley during the Boer siege of 1899 to 1900. He tells the story week by week, in eighteen chapters, from October 1899 onward. Shelling, shortage, and martial law form the backdrop, but Phelan stresses humour and social life. Concerts, gossip, and blunders by clerks and officers lighten grim days.

Phelan watches raw recruits, seasoned campaigners, and townspeople with a comic eye. He records how laughter itself risked punishment under martial law. As a siege diary, it is vivid and humane. It shows ordinary people keeping spirits up under fire.
17824-little-black-sambo:
Helen Bannerman wrote Little Black Sambo as a small picture tale, here printed by Saalfield with pictures by Florence White Williams. A little boy in fine new clothes walks out in the jungle and meets a tiger.

To save himself, Sambo gives the tiger his coat, then his trousers, shoes, and umbrella, one by one. At last the tigers chase each other round a tree and melt into butter. The tale's words and pictures now read as dated and hurtful caricature. Modern readers meet it mainly as a relic of its age, not as a book to give a child.
26672-bookbinding-and-the-care-of-books-:
Douglas Cockerell wrote this handbook for amateurs, bookbinders, and librarians, published by D. Appleton at New York in 1910 in the Artistic Crafts Series edited by W. R. Lethaby. Drawings by Noel Rooke illustrate workshop practice. Lethaby's preface argues that design cannot be detached from workmanship, and that ornament is pleasant thought voiced in the tool's own speech.

Part one teaches binding step by step, including rounding, which controls the swelling of the back into an even convex form, and backing, which grooves the boards to fit neatly. Cockerell's note hopes to help binders and librarians choose sound methods. It is a craftsman's manual from the Ruskin and Morris tradition, valuing good material, contrivance, and finish over mere appearance.
30011-an-aviator-s-field-book-being-the-:
Oswald Bolcke's field reports run from August 1, 1914, to October 28, 1916, translated from the German by Robert Reynold Hirsch, with a foreword by Joseph E. Ridder. The National Military Publishing Company of New York printed the book in 1917. Colonel Bolcke's last picture fronts the volume, and pictures of his first victory, an enemy aeroplane in ruins, and his men follow.

Bolcke and his brother Wilhelm appear in September 1914, and Bolcke and his brother Max in France in August 1916. A picture of his last ride, on October 28, 1916, at five in the afternoon, closes the plates. Ridder says Bolcke wrote daily impressions to keep in touch with his people and quiet their fears, without boasting, modestly and naturally. The book is a first-hand record of a knight of the air in the Great War.
32916-a-secret-of-the-lebombo:
Bertram Mitford opens on a hot afternoon in a green and gold valley, where a farmer named Wyvern tracks sheep-stealers. From a perch above a donga he watches two men butchering one of his own sheep. One wears greasy moleskin trousers on braces repaired with string; the other wears only a string of blue beads. Wyvern recognizes the first as one of his own herdsmen.

The pair are two to one against an unarmed man carrying only a pocket knife, and a recent murder of a stock farmer under similar circumstances is fresh in Wyvern's mind. He must decide whether to withdraw and lay a trap. The wider story draws in Lalante, whom Wyvern loves, and Joe Fleetwood, a shrewd practical man whose instincts warn him that an effusive host means mischief. Slaves cutting wood in a sombre forest mark the host's true character.
36398-ruth-fielding-at-silver-ranch-or-s:
Ruth Fielding at Silver Ranch, or Schoolgirls among the Cowboys, by Alice Emerson, is a girls’ story of 1918. Cupples and Leon of New York published the book. A front plate shows a horse called Freckles leaping up, frightened and snorting. Emerson had written Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill before it.

Ruth Fielding at Briarwood Hall and Ruth Fielding at Snow Camp stand in the series list. This volume takes Ruth and her friends west to a ranch. Cowboys, roundups, and ranch perils replace the campus of the earlier books. Emerson ground out the Ruth Fielding line for years of girl readers. The west tests her schoolgirl heroines in saddle and corral. Clean adventure and loyal friendship are the series promise.
45811-a-chesterton-calendar-compiled-fro:
A Chesterton Calendar gathers short pieces from the writings of Chesterton, in verse and prose, one for each day, with a part apart for moveable feasts. The book was published in London in 1911. A prefatory note says almost all of Chesterton's books were used, with thanks to many publishers and to the Daily News and Illustrated London News.

New pieces appear by Chesterton's own leave, from poems not yet printed in full. January opens with his scorn for mere light sophistry, drawn from Orthodoxy. For New Year's Day he argues that a new year aims not at a new year but at a new soul, new feet, new eyes, and a fresh start on life. Wit and faith mark the daily fare.
48548-further-remarks-on-the-policy-of-l:
Henry W Chandler wrote Further Remarks on lending Bodleian books. B H Blackwell issued the pamphlet at Oxford in 1887. It sold for sixpence at the time. Chandler was a curator of the Bodleian Library. He taught moral philosophy at Oxford as well. Pembroke College held his fellowship then.

He doubts he will speak in the statute debate, he opens. Yet he keeps the right to answer print claims, he says. Lending's friends would change the library's whole character, he charges. A reference library would turn circulating in their plan. They shun the facts of the case, he claims. Side issues fill their letters instead, he says. The Advocates' Library lends its books in Scotland. It had lost many by 1852, he notes. A curator's brief against lending shows the old research libraries guarding their shelves in the age of the public library.
49057-tales-of-king-arthur-and-the-round:
Tales of King Arthur and the Round Table retells the Arthur legends from Andrew Lang's Book of Romance. Allen shaped it for Longmans' class-books of English literature, with opening words, notes, and twenty pictures by Ford. Longmans issued this new impression in 1918 from London, New York, Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.

Part one tells the drawing of the sword, Excalibur, and the start of the Round Table. The story of Sir Balin, Beaumains at court, and Morgan le Fay's plot against Arthur follow, ending with the passing of Merlin. Part two gives the quest of the Holy Graal. Later parts tell the fight for the queen, the fair maid of Astolat, Lancelot and Guenevere, and the end of it all.
52465-the-faithful-servant-a-sermon-prea:
The Faithful Servant is a sermon preached in St Peter, Southborough, on the death of the Reverend Stephen Langston, late vicar of that parish. The preacher was Canon Hoare, vicar of Trinity, Tunbridge Wells. The pamphlet was published in London and Tunbridge Wells in 1879.

The text is from Matthew: well done, good and faithful servant. Thou hast been faithful over a few things; I will make thee ruler over many things. Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord. There is something very solemn in the death of any one, Hoare opens. It is peculiarly solemn in the death of a minister of God. When he dies he resigns not his life only, but his ministry. He gives back the ministerial trust committed to him. Readers get a Victorian funeral sermon for a parish priest.
53011-the-mentor-a-little-book-for-the-g:
Alfred Ayres wrote The Mentor as a little book for the guidance of such men and boys as would appear to advantage in society. The advertisements bound before it list his other manuals, which explain the Mentor's trade: Ayres taught Americans how to speak and behave.

Some Ill-used Words, his manual for those who desire to write and speak correctly, sold for a dollar. The Orthoëpist, a pronouncing manual of some four thousand five hundred words, cost a dollar and a quarter. The Verbalist treated the right and wrong use of words. Ayres, whose real name was Osmun, was the self-appointed umpire of American usage. The Mentor extends his jurisdiction from the tongue to the whole man: dress, address, and deportment, corrected for climbers who meant to arrive.
54051-the-book-of-the-sailboat-how-to-ri:
A Hyatt Verrill teaches small-boat handling in an Appleton handbook from New York and London dated 1916. A front plate sorts fore-and-aft sails and rigs in eleven forms, from leg-o'-mutton and lateen to sloop and yawl. Verrill had written on motor boats and whalers before this guide.

Chapter one gives a short history of boats, from rafts and canoes to schooners, sloops, and catboats. Chapter two weighs speed, steadiness, and seaworthiness to help a buyer pick a boat for a set use. Whale-boats, dories, skip-jacks, and oyster boats each get a plain word on their merits. Later chapters name each part of hull, mast, and rigging and tell what each part is for.
54895-limbo:
Aldous Huxley gathers early fiction in Limbo, published at London by Chatto and Windus in 1920. The longest piece, Farcical History of Richard Greenow, runs past a hundred pages, followed by Happily Ever After and Eupompus Gave Splendour to Art by Numbers. Shorter pieces called Happy Families, Cynthia, The Bookshop and The Death of Lully complete the volume.

Richard Greenow's story opens with his sister Millicent's seventh birthday and a sumptuous doll's house from the immensely rich Aunty Loo. Millicent, who had prayed for a working toy sewing-machine, ignores the present, while Dick spends hours rearranging its furniture in secret.
57637-zigzag-journeys-in-the-white-city-:
Hezekiah Butterworth wrote this tour book in his long Zigzag Journeys set for youth. The book came out in 1894 and treats the White City fair. Front pages list past trips in the set, from Europe to India. Each past book took young travelers to a new famed place.

The White City was the great Chicago fair of that era. Butterworth guides readers through its halls and nearby sights in turn. The tone is bright, plain, and full of facts for youth. Readers get a guided walk through a fair that awed its age.
59456-fors-clavigera-volume-1-of-8-lette:
Fors Clavigera is a series of letters by John Ruskin, addressed to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain. George Allen published the first volume at Orpington in 1871. Ruskin held the Slade chair of fine art at Oxford at the time. The letters were issued one by one as a running public address.

The first letter is dated from Denmark Hill on New Year's Day, 1871. Ruskin tells his readers that Britain begins a new decade in unhappy shape. The country has escaped the disasters that fell on its neighbours in war. That escape, he insists, owes nothing to better desert or wisdom. He charges his countrymen with fear before nearly every nation on earth. The root fault, he says, is a national wish to get gain from others.
61591-fors-clavigera-volume-2-of-8-lette:
The second volume of Fors Clavigera gathers John Ruskin's letters to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain. George Allen published it at Orpington in 1872. Ruskin was then Slade Professor of Fine Art at Oxford. Letter Thirteen, dated the first of January 1872, opens the volume with a refusal. Ruskin will not wish his readers a happy New Year, since his wishes have mostly proved vain and made him wretched.

He advises them instead to wish to deserve a happy New Year, whether they get one or not. Talk of deserving, he argues, not of rights: a man may deserve a whipping, but no one says he has a right to one. The letter takes up Carlyle's sentence on rights and mights in The French Revolution. Ruskin defends it: force of brains, force of heart, and force of hand are what men must worship, he says, not weakness.
61634-fors-clavigera-volume-3-of-8-lette:
Fors Clavigera, volume three, gathers John Ruskin's letters to British workmen. George Allen of Orpington, Kent, put the volume out in 1873. Ruskin was Slade Professor of Fine Art and an Oxford honorary student. Letter twenty-five opens this third volume, dated January 4, 1873. Brantwood, his home by the lake, heads the New Year's letter here.

The Third Fors had turned his good printer adrift, Ruskin complains. That misfortune left the letter a fortnight late for its readers. A cookery book of 1791 consoles him with a goose pie receipt. Yorkshire goose pie opens his economical instructions for the current year. Fairy butter and an apple floating-island tempt him sorely aside first. Take a large fat goose, split it down the back, the receipt runs. A brown-bread oven must be built before the pie can be made.
62710-king-mombo:
King Mombo, a tale of Africa by Paul Du Chaillu, was published at London in 1902. John Murray issued it with illustrations by Victor Perard that year. Du Chaillu wrote The Viking Age and Explorations in Equatorial Africa, the title page lists. A front plate shows natives asking if the travellers want to barter for ivory.

A letter to a Philadelphia doctor opens the book in place of a preface. Du Chaillu looks back through the vista of years to his broken health, he writes. Care and skill had restored him and let him resume his work in those days. Gorilla country, forest peoples, and trade on the rivers of west Africa fill the tale. Boys of 1902 met the jungle through his mix of travel fact and story.
62971-the-adventures-of-a-woman-hobo:
Ethel Lynn, a doctor, wrote the true tale of her tramp life, printed at New York in 1917. It opens as a diary at Chicago on April 18 1908. That day a fellow doctor told her she had the first stage of consumption. He ordered her back to California at once.

She could not grasp it, for she had worked since she was fifteen. She built a city practice by her own hands after medical school. Two years before, the San Francisco quake and fire had wrecked that practice. Her husband Dan lost his post too, and the panic of 1907 crushed his hopes of backing for his new device.
64700-fombombo:
T S Stribling sends an American drummer into Venezuelan revolution country in a novel issued by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1923. The Century Company holds the copyright. Stribling dedicates it to his uncle, a soldier, fox-hunter, and philosopher.

Chapter one opens at the American Consulate in Caracas. Thomas Strawbridge calls from a sense of duty. The consul, a weary politician from Kentucky, serves gin and cigars. He asks if Strawbridge is one of the Strawbridges of Virginia. The young man lives in Keokuk, Iowa, and knows little of his roots. Talk turns to Venezuela sweltering outside. Both men damn the place thoroughly. Strawbridge preaches his creed elsewhere: the fellow who pulls slick stuff in a business deal has hit the chutes for the bowwows. Business honesty, he insists, wins in the long run.
67142-lost-with-lieutenant-pike-how-from:
Edwin Sabin wrote a boys' tale of Pike's march, printed in 1919 in a set called the American Trail Blazers. The set tells true parts of early American history as stirring tales. Each book takes one great man or one great event. Colour and black drawings fill the pages.

The long title tells the plot. A boy named Scar Head marches from the Pawnee village with the young chief Pike into the snowy mountains. In the dead of winter they hunt the lost river and think they have found it. Then Spanish soldiers take them down to Santa Fe, where one more surprise waits. The book is given to the men who served in 1917 and 1918.
67324-placebo:
David Mason's short story from Infinity Science Fiction in November nineteen fifty five opens with a machine materializing on a street called Main Way. A barefoot philosopher named Philip Corrigan watches it arrive without surprise. The young man in the saddle seat is Darwin Lenner, a time traveler. He has just left the year nineteen fifty five four times, and each version was worse than the last.

Now the machine will not work. Lenner learns that Corrigan can read his thoughts, and that Corrigan still doubts time travel is possible at all. Mason builds the story as a talk between the stranded traveler and the calm local who may know more than he says. The premise turns the usual time machine tale sideways. The future that produced Lenner is not obviously better than the placid place he has landed in.
67544-fors-clavigera-volume-4-of-8-lette:
John Ruskin's Fors Clavigera, letters to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain, reaches volume four with George Allen of Orpington, Kent, in 1874. Ruskin signs himself an honorary student of Christ Church and Slade professor of fine art. Letter thirty-seven is dated the first of January, 1874.

The letter opens with an old French poem on perfect charity, Englished line by line beneath it. Who loves God, it says, loves his neighbour. No man can call a thing his own beyond what he has put into that good. Ruskin then turns to a small Oxford scene. On his way to lecture on the fine arts in Florence, he watched a little girl whip a top in a pair of cast-off shoes far too big for her feet.
68013-fors-clavigera-volume-5-of-8-lette:
John Ruskin published the fifth volume of his letters to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain at Orpington in 1875. Ruskin was Slade professor of fine art at Oxford. Letter forty nine opens the volume. He wonders if Fors will let him say any small part of what he intends this year. His readers, he admits, have a right to doubt his plan.

To define the plan severely would falsify it, Ruskin argues. All that is best in it depends on taking up whatever good he finds in men and things. It is not a plan or scheme at all, he corrects himself. It is only a method. The Fors letters ran for years.
7297-the-vedanta-sutras-with-the-comment:
George Thibaut translates the Vedanta Sutras with Ramanuja's commentary in this third part of the Sacred Books of the East, volume forty-eight, published in 1904. Its contents run through four chapters, each in four parts, with an introduction, moving stepwise through the aphorisms that sum up Vedanta teaching and the great commentator's reading of them.

Ramanuja's voice guides the reader through dense, brief sutras, opening each knot of doctrine with reason and scripture. Thibaut's English keeps the argument orderly, so that a Western reader can follow a system built on terse lines and long debate. The volume stands as a bridge between Indian philosophy and English scholarship.
76792-hurlothrumbo:
Hurlothrumbo, or The Super Natural is a play by Samuel Johnson of Cheshire, acted at the New Theatre in the Hay Market. It was printed in London for the author in MDCCXXIX, and reprinted in Dublin the same year. Johnson gave the play to Lady Delves for her care. The title page bids the sons of fire to read it and be struck dumb.

Johnson was known as a famed odd wit, dancer, and fiddler of his day. His play mixes high claims with low jokes and strange super natural turns. The text keeps old spelling and caps as first printed. Readers of stage lore will value it as a famed odd piece that drew crowds and much talk in its time. It shows what London playgoers would cheer in that age.
9256-the-paradise-of-children-from-a-won:
Hawthorne's Paradise of Children, from A Wonder-Book, opens in the Tanglewood playroom at Christmas. Golden October passed, brown November too, and most of chill December, till merry Christmas brought Eustace Bright from college. The next day a mighty snowstorm came, after mild days like smiles on winter's wrinkled face.

Grass stayed green in sheltered nooks, along lee stone fences, till snow closed the scene. Then Eustace tells the children of Pandora and the paradise lost. Hawthorne's frame and myth join winter cheer to ancient wonder. The tale remains a favorite Christmas retelling for young readers.
britannica-1911-bilbo:
Bilbo takes its name from Bilbao in Spain, once written Bilboa in England. That town, like Toledo, was famous for its sword blades. In the earliest English use, a bilbo was a sword, one of superior temper especially. The word then shifted to a very different object of iron. Shakespeare uses the plural, bilboes, in a well-known phrase about lying worse than the mutines in the bilboes.

In that plural sense bilboes were the irons fitted on board ship. Offenders were locked into them as a punishment afloat. The 1911 Britannica entry is only a few lines long. It gives the Spanish source of the word, the sword sense, and the shipboard irons sense. It quotes Shakespeare's line as its one piece of evidence. No dates for the word's first use are supplied in the entry.
britannica-1911-carabobo:
Carabobo is a state of Venezuela, in South America. It is the smallest of the country's thirteen states. Its area is 2985 square miles. Its population was estimated at 221,891 in 1905. This 1911 Britannica entry surveys its land and products. The Caribbean Sea bounds it to the north. Aragua lies east, Zamora south, and Lara west. Most of its surface is mountainous.

South of the Cordillera, wide grassy plains stretch out. Great herds of cattle graze those plains. The higher valleys grow coffee and cereals. The lower valleys, near Lake Valencia, grow sugar. The coast yields cacao and coco-nuts of fine quality. Minerals are worked in the south-west, near Nirgua. Valencia is the capital of the state. Puerto Cabello is its chief port town. The state is best known for a great battle. It was fought on a plain there on 24 June 1821.
britannica-1911-carbo:
Carbo was the name of a Roman family. It belonged to the Papirian gens, a plebeian house. This 1911 Britannica article treats its leading members. The first is Gaius Papirius Carbo, a statesman and orator. He worked with Gaius Gracchus on the land laws. As tribune in 131 B.C. he carried a ballot law. It extended voting by ballot to the making of laws.

Carbo was suspected in the sudden death of Scipio. That suspicion hung over him from 129 B.C. He later crossed over to the optimates, the senatorial party. As consul in 120 he defended Lucius Opimius in court. Opimius stood accused over the killing of citizens. Carbo even said Gracchus had been justly slain. The optimates never trusted the turncoat, though. Licinius Crassus impeached him on a like charge. Facing certain condemnation, Carbo took his own life. The article then turns to his son, surnamed Arvina.
britannica-1911-coquimbo:
Coquimbo, a city and port of Chile, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands in the province and department of the same name. Its people numbered 7,322 in 1895. Rail lines link it with Ovalle to the south and Vicuña to the east. A planned line northward would tie it directly to Santiago.

The city has a good, well-sheltered harbour. It is reputed the best in northern Chile. Coquimbo is the port of La Serena, the provincial capital. La Serena lies nine miles away and is joined by rail. Large copper-smelting works stand in the city. It exports a very large amount of copper. Some gold and silver go out as well. Cattle and hay go to the more northern provinces. The article then turns to the province of Coquimbo itself. Trade readers get a mining port and its hinterland in one sketch.
britannica-1911-emmius-ubbo:
Emmius, Ubbo (1547–1625), was a Dutch historian and geographer born at Gretha in East Friesland on 5 December 1547. After study at Rostock he spent two years in Geneva and grew close to Theodore Beza. Back in the Netherlands he became principal of a college at Norden. He lost that post in 1587 because, as a Calvinist, he would not sign the confession of Augsburg.

Emmius next headed a college at Leer, and in 1594 became rector of the college at Groningen. When that college became a university in 1614, he was chosen its principal and professor of history and Greek. By wise guidance and learning he soon raised the new university to high standing. He died at Groningen on 9 December 1625. His chief works include the Rerum Frisicarum historiae decades, a full edition of which appeared at Leiden in 1616. His Opus chronologicum came out in 1619, and his Vetus Graecia illustrata in 1626.
britannica-1911-gazebo:
Gazebo, in the 1911 Britannica, is a short word entry about a garden building. The word was used in the 18th century for a structure set on the outer wall of a garden. Its upper storey had windows on each side, so that those inside could overlook the road.

The name is usually explained as a comic Latinism, as if from 'I will gaze.' The New English Dictionary, the entry notes, suggests instead a possible oriental origin, now lost. Similar buildings stand in Holland along the canals, where in some cases they make very picturesque features. The notice is brief: a definition, a guess at the word's birth, and a Dutch parallel.
britannica-1911-godfrey-of-viterbo:
Godfrey of Viterbo is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a writer of chronicles from about 1120 to about 1196. He was most likely Italian by birth, some say Saxon. He spent early life and his last days at Viterbo. He was schooled at Bamberg and learned Latin well. About 1140 he became chaplain to a German king. Most of his life was spent as a secretary.

He served the emperor Frederick the First in that post. The emperor trusted him and sent him on many missions. Those trips took him to Sicily, France, and Spain. He stood by the emperor in drives in Italy. After the emperor death he kept favour with his son. For that son he wrote a mirror for kings. That work is held to be of little worth. A world chronicle of his is told in prose and verse.
britannica-1911-nebo:
Nebo, also called Nabu, meaning the proclaimer, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Nebo was one of the chief gods of the Babylonian pantheon. The main seat of his worship was at Borsippa, across from the city of Babylon. As Babylon became the centre of empire, Borsippa grew close to it. Through that link, the cult of Nebo kept a standing just below that of Marduk.

The friendly tie between the two gods was shown by making Nebo the son of Marduk. That form marked the superiority of Marduk over his son. Borsippa in time became a mere adjunct of Babylon, yet the Nebo cult was never fully absorbed. The article gives a reason for that survival. Nebo had become the god of wisdom, credited with bringing in writing. His wisdom dealt much with reading the movements of the heavens.
britannica-1911-shwebo:
Shwebo is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and district in Upper Burma. The town stands in a rice plain north east of Mandalay. A count from 1901 gives the town 9626 people. The district held far more, near 287 thousand in all. The town is famed as the birthplace of Alompra. He founded the last Burmese dynasty and made it his capital.

After British rule took hold, the town held a large camp. By the time of the entry, only part of a regiment stayed. The Irrawaddy river forms the east edge of the district. The Minwun hills run down that same side. Land in the middle rises in a slow slope. The Mu river cuts through the centre of the district. Rice land fills much of the plain.
britannica-1911-strabo:
Strabo, a Greek writer on lands and the past, opens a long life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Amasia in Pontus near sixty three before Christ, he was Greek in speech and schooling. His mother kin held high posts under the kings of Pontus. He learned at Nysa, at Rome, and with wise men at Alexandria. Books of Aristotle were part of his study at Rome.

Few dates of his life can be fixed with care, the text says. He stood at Gyaros when Augustus passed in twenty nine before Christ. He sailed with a Roman chief up the Nile to Syene and Philae. His own words claim wide trips from Etruria to the edge of Ethiopia. Yet he saw but a small part of the lands his great work maps.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aegidius-of-v:
Aegidius of Viterbo, cardinal, theologian, orator, humanist, and poet, was born at Viterbo in Italy and died at Rome on 12 November 1532. He joined the Augustinian Order young and became its general. He is famous for the bold, earnest discourse he gave at the Fifth General Council's Lateran opening in 1512, printed in Harduin's collection of councils.

Leo X made him cardinal, gave him several sees in succession, used him as legate on important missions, granting him in 1523 the Latin Patriarch of Constantinople title. His zeal for genuine reform prompted a Promemoria to Adrian VI on ecclesiastical conditions. He was universally esteemed as learned and virtuous, and many saw him as Clement VII's destined successor. A profound student of scripture and scholar in Greek and Hebrew, he feared, when urged to publish, contradicting famous and holy men by his exposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambo:
The ambo, plural ambos or ambones, is a Greek word taken to mean a mountain or elevation, as Innocent III understood it. Ambones likely grew from the raised platform where Jewish rabbis read Scripture to the people. They entered churches in the fourth century, were universal by the ninth, and reached full flowering and artistic beauty in the twelfth. Then they gradually fell from use.

An ambo is a raised desk or pulpit where Gospel and Epistle were sung or read and notices given to the congregation. Bishops sometimes preached from it, as John Chrysostom mounting it to be heard distinctly. The deacon ascending to read the Gospel recalled Isaiah's call to climb a high mountain bringing good tidings to Sion, and Christ preaching from a mountain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annius-of-vit:
Annius of Viterbo, born Giovanni Nanni, scholar of old Rome, born about 1432, died 1502. He joined the Dominicans early. Sixtus IV and Alexander VI held him in high esteem, and made him Sacred Palace Master. Skilled in Eastern tongues and fond of old Rome, he took a Golden Age name. His books include De futuris Christianorum triumphis, notes on John's vision, and Tractatus de imperio Turcorum, Genoa, 1480.

He is best known for Antiquitatum Variarum, Venice, 1499. In it he put out old writings said to be from writers before Christ, shedding new light on old history. He said he found them in Mantua. The book met fans and foes who said he made it up. These works have long been seen as fakes, though he thought them true. His books not yet in print include one on Etruscan old things and his Chronologia Nova, fixing date slips in church books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aribo:
Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, whose birth date is unknown and who died on 6 April 1032, was one of the most prominent churchmen of his time. Son of Arbo, palatine count in Laubenthal, and Adela, he became deacon at Salzburg, then chaplain to his kinsman Emperor Henry II, who appointed him to Mainz. His consecration took place on 1 October 1021 with great pomp.

The next year he revived the famous Gandersheim dispute over rival claims of Hildesheim's bishops and Mainz's archbishops to jurisdiction over Gandersheim convent. It lay on the diocesan border, though long subject to Hildesheim. Having pressed his claim without success at Frankfurt in 1027 and Poehlde in 1029, Aribo renounced it at Merseburg in 1030, admitting error and promising silence. He also figured prominently in politics after Henry II's death ended the Saxon male line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernabe-cobo:
Bernabé Cobo, a Jesuit missionary and historian of the Americas, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Lopera in Spain in 1582, he died at Lima in 1657 after sailing to America in 1596 and joining the Jesuits in 1601. Missions at Juli, Potosí, Cochabamba, Oruro, and La Paz filled his early years.

College rectorships at Arequipa, Pisco, and Callao followed, then a long stay in Mexico until 1650 and a return to Peru. His great history of the New World, drawing on years of travel and reading, is his monument. The entry laments that later centuries neglected a writer of such wide American knowledge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-crisp:
Blessed Crispin of Viterbo, a Capuchin lay brother, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Viterbo in 1668, he died at Rome in 1750. At five his pious mother took him to a shrine of the Virgin near Viterbo and consecrated him to Mary. Townsfolk called the virtuous child il Santarello, the little saint.

Seeing Capuchin novices in procession stirred him to religious life, and he was received as a simple lay brother, modelling himself on St. Felix of Cantalice and calling himself the order's ass of burden. Asked why he went bare-headed, he joked that an ass wears no hat. Sent to Rome in feeble old age, he died there, his body still preserved under a Capuchin altar, and Pius VII beatified him in 1806.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colombo:
Antony Coudert's entry follows the Archdiocese of Colombo on Ceylon's western seaboard. It takes in two of the island's nine provinces, the Western and the Northwestern. Its history opens in 1518, when Franciscans brought Christianity. The faith spread fast, and the town and nearby districts soon formed a diocese. Don Juan de Monteiro became its first bishop. He received into the Church the prince Don Juan Dharmapala, grandson of King Buwenekabahu VII.

That prince took the throne in 1542. Six years later Colombo held 12,000 Catholics, with two parish churches, four houses of friars, and a Jesuit college. Dharmapala died in 1597, and Dutch rule later left the island to the Bishop of Cochin. Gregory XVI restored its own structure in 1830. A further split in 1883 set Colombo apart from Kandy. By the last census the archdiocese held 1,274,000 people, of whom 206,000 were Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ebbo:
Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, was born toward the end of the eighth century of German serfs and died on 20 March 851. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Charlemagne schooled him at court and gave him freedom. After ordination he served as librarian and councillor to Louis the Pious in Aquitaine, and when Louis became emperor he named Ebbo to the vacant see of Reims in 816.

At the emperor's urging Ebbo went to Rome in 822 for leave from Pope Paschal the First to preach to the Danes. The pope not only agreed but made him legate for the North. With Halitgar and Willerich he sailed for Denmark in spring 823 and preached with some success. Deposed and restored in later strife, he wrote his own Apology, preserved by Mansi and Migne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-of-vi:
Godfrey of Viterbo was a German writer of the twelfth century, whose birthplace and birth date are unknown. Taken by Lothair to Bamberg in 1133, he was educated there. He then served as clergy at the courts of Conrad III and later Frederick I, following the latter on many campaigns and on frequent diplomatic missions. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a court notary and chaplain of forty years.

For his court services he received lands in fief at Viterbo, probably in 1169. He spent his last days there, though his death year is unknown. About 1183 he compiled the Speculum regum, a world history from the Deluge meant to reconcile Romans and Germans. His Memoria Saeculorum was finished in 1185, and his Pantheon, begun the same year, won unmerited fame in the Middle Ages for its fables and folklore material.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lavabo:
Lavabo names the hand-washing at Mass after the Offertory, from the first word of the Psalm 25 passage the celebrant says while washing. Hand-washing before the liturgy began as plain cleanliness, then gained symbolic sense, and appears in every rite.

Eastern rites wash at vesting, usually with the same psalm fragment, while Apostolic Constitutions place a washing before the catechumens' dismissal and Syrian and Coptic rites after the creed. Rome washed before vesting with another prayer, and added the Mass washing from sheer need after receiving the people's loaves and wine vessels at the Offertory. Early Roman ordines show celebrant and deacons washing right after carrying offerings to the altar, with no psalm or prayer yet attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limbo:
Limbo, Late Latin limbus, is a Teutonic word meaning hem or border. In theological use the name is given to two states. The limbus patrum is the temporary place or state of the just who, though purified from sin, were shut out from the beatific vision until Christ's ascension into Heaven. The limbus infantium or puerorum is the permanent place or state of unbaptized children and others dying without grievous sin. Original sin alone shuts them out from the beatific vision.

Of the limbus patrum, writings outside the canon, from the second or first centuries B.C., repeatedly voice some such belief, and New Testament references confirm the Jewish belief in Christ's time. In the New Testament, Christ speaks of it as a banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and a marriage feast for the prudent virgins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mateo-realdo-:
Mateo Realdo Colombo was an Italian anatomist and discoverer of the pulmonary circulation, born at Cremona in 1516 and dead at Rome in 1559. In 1545 Cosimo de' Medici, reorganising Pisa University, lured him as first anatomy professor there.

Through Padua, Pisa, and Rome teaching he pursued original anatomy research, published as De Re Anatomica Libri XV at Venice in 1559. Its chief feature is an accurate, complete account of pulmonary circulation. Blood goes through the artery-like vein into the lungs, thins there, and comes back, carrying air, through the vein-like artery into the left ventricle of the heart. Colombo knew this was original, writing that no one had yet observed or recorded it. Harvey quoted him more than once and credited his many original findings, though English medical writers often slighted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-nebo:
Mount Nebo is a mountain of the Abarim range east of Jordan and the Dead Sea. From it Moses surveyed the Promised Land, and there he died, as Deuteronomy 32 and 34 relate. The same name may appear in the wanderings of Numbers 33, though there the reference could be to the town of Nebo instead.

Its exact site is doubtful. Comparing Deuteronomy 3 with Deuteronomy 32 suggests that the top of Pisgah and Nebo were variant names for one spot. Yet no point in the Abarim range seems to command all the territory Deuteronomy 34 lists, especially if the furthermost sea means the Mediterranean. Some identify Nebo with the modern Jebel Neba, an oblong ridge five miles southwest of Heshbon, 2,700 feet above sea level.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nabo-nebo:
Nabo, or Nebo, is a town mentioned in several Old Testament passages, including Numbers 32, Jeremiah 48, First Chronicles 5 and Isaiah 15. In Numbers 32 it appears between Saban and Beon, the latter an abbreviation of Baalmeon. It appears again between Cariathaim and Baalmeon, and with the same neighbours on the Mesa Stone.

Those signs place the town near Mount Nebo, though its precise site cannot be fixed. It belonged to the rich pasture lands the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked of Moses in the distribution of territory. By the time Isaiah prophesied against it, the town had reverted to the Moabites. Mesa boasts of taking it from the Israelites. According to Saint Jerome, the sanctuary of the idol Chemosh stood in Nabo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-bembo:
Pietro Bembo was a Venetian scholar, courtier, and cardinal whose polished Latin and Italian set the standard of style for his age. He was born at Venice in 1470 and studied Greek at Messina and philosophy at Padua. He shone at the courts of Ferrara and Urbino, and in 1512 became secretary to Pope Leo X at Rome.

After Leo's death he retired to Padua, gathering a great library and a museum of medals and antiquities. That house drew Italy's learned men to him. He served Venice as historian and librarian of Saint Mark's. He received the cardinal's hat in 1539 and turned from classics to the church fathers and Scripture. He died at Rome in 1547 as bishop of Bergamo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastiano-de:
Sebastiano del Piombo, more correctly Sebastiano Luciani, was a Venetian portrait painter born at Venice in 1485 who died at Rome in 1547. He took his name del Piombo from the office Clement VII gave him as keeper of the leaden seals. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a musician turned painter.

A pupil of Giovanni Bellini and later of Giorgione, he first meant to become a priest, likely took minor orders, and planned ordination. But love of music absorbed him, and through music he met Giorgione, a clever musician, who persuaded him to delay priesthood and try painting. On Giorgione's advice he entered Bellini's studio, then worked in Giorgione's own studio, and from that friendship his church career faded. Chigi later invited him to Rome, where his career flourished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-of-:
St. Colman of Templeshambo was a Connacht saint, confounded with the patron of Kilmacduagh, but he lived somewhat earlier. The sphere of his ministry lay in the present County Wexford. This entry follows a man of Saint Aidan's time, whom Aidan made Abbot of Templeshambo, Enniscorthy's mother church. Many legends are told of Colman and of his holy well with its sacred ducks.

Certain it is, however, that he worked zealously at Mount Leinster's foot, his monastery called Temple Sean Bothe. He died about 595 on 27 October, the day the Martyrology of Donegal records his feast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rose-of-vi:
Rose of Viterbo, a child preacher of penance, defied an emperor's prefect and foretold his death. Born at Viterbo in 1235 to poor and pious parents, she showed holiness and miraculous power from her earliest years. At three she reportedly raised her maternal aunt to life, and at seven she lived as a recluse given to penance.

Cured by the Virgin, she joined the Third Order of Francis and preached penance through Viterbo, then held by Frederick II and torn by strife and heresy. Her success threatened imperial power, and in January 1250 she and her parents were expelled to Soriano. On 5 December she foretold Frederick's speedy death, fulfilled on 13 December. She died on 6 March 1252, aged only seventeen.
doe-osti-17076277-development-of-the-ari:
Oak Ridge led a four site team that began building the ARISE outreach dashboard in fiscal 2026, reported in September 2026. Paco Parada and colleagues from Oak Ridge worked with Y-12, Sandia, and Lawrence Livermore staff. ARISE, the Advanced Reactors International Safeguards Engagement program, needed one shared view of its ties with United States advanced reactor companies.

Fiscal 2026 delivered a pilot version and a plan for gathering open source data to fill it. A scraping approach, which collects web data automatically, was built with update automation and confidence markings on gathered values. Full deployment, scaling, and feedback rounds with the sponsoring headquarters office are planned for fiscal 2027.
doe-osti-3029078-systems-biology-to-enab:
Jamey D Young of Vanderbilt University led project DE-SC0022207, reported April 7, 2026, with John A McLean, Brian F Pfleger of Wisconsin, and Doug K Allen of the Danforth Center. The team engineered the cyanobacterium Picosynechococcus strain PCC 7002 to make free fatty acids, feedstocks for fuels and oleochemicals, treating its metabolism as modules upstream and downstream of acetyl-CoA. Finding which module throttles output was the systems biology task.

A production platform came from deleting the acyl-ACP synthetase gene and expressing a modified Cuphea palustris thioesterase, yielding eight-carbon fatty acids. Pooled CRISPR interference screens then hunted helpful knockdowns under working conditions. At high cell density, enriched guide targets included photosynthesis and energy genes such as psbL and ndhF and the translation factor prfC; a screen under four percent carbon dioxide pointed elsewhere.
doe-osti-3374009-arch-technology-snapsho:
Los Alamos National Laboratory technology snapshot LA-UR-26-24876, issued June 12, 2026, by Dharmesh N. Patel, presents ARCH, the Autonomous Robot Control Hierarchy. ARCH is a shared software system for robots, built so teams do not have to rebuild robot software each time the platform or the task changes. Swapping a sensor or moving to a different robot now forces months of fresh coding, and the snapshot pitches ARCH as the fix.

ARCH grew out of autonomous radiation survey work at Los Alamos, where several sensors, heavy data flow, and steady real-time control were all required. The system is built from reusable parts that link sensors, robot platforms, algorithms, and tasks in one consistent way. Developers can then carry proven pieces from one robot to the next instead of starting over.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HBO_HBO: nsia-HBO HBO: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-book-of-veles-be: The Book of Veles claims to be an ancient Slavic text, written on wooden planks and lost in the twentieth century. Scholars widely regard it as a modern forgery. The library presents it as an archive holding, without endorsement. Its real interest is modern: a fake scripture can still found real movements. The book documents how badly some readers want an ancient past, and what they will accept as proof of one.
govdocs-archive_org-the-legacy-of-our-an: The Legacy of Our Ancestors follows Germanic festivals and customs through the turning year. It moves from winter solstice and carnival through the spring and harvest feasts. Folk calendars tie a people's work, weather, and worship into one round of days. The volume records those customs in order, season by season. It serves readers of folklore who want the old Germanic year laid out whole rather than in scattered notes.
little-black-sambo:
Helen Bannerman tells this picture story of a small boy in India. Saalfield Publishing issued this edition with Florence White Williams's illustrations. His mother, Black Mumbo, makes him a beautiful red coat. She adds a pair of beautiful blue trousers for him.

His father, Black Jumbo, buys gifts at the bazaar. A green umbrella and purple shoes with crimson soles arrive. The opening pages dress Sambo proudly for his walk. The book's period language reflects its original era plainly. The Saalfield edition prints the tale as a picture book. Each short line faces its own illustration for young readers.
nasa-tm-19680024812-static-oxidation-and:
John D. Buckley of Langley Research Center tested boron nitride at extreme heat in this paper, presented in April 1968. Two grades of boron nitride and one boron nitride composite went through the tests. Boron nitride is a ceramic valued for surviving very high temperatures.

Samples sat in air at high heat and in vacuum at still higher heat for varied times. Compatibility tests paired the materials with refractory oxides, a graphite composite, and refractory metals. Results showed composition shapes thermal shock and oxidation resistance. Little or no reaction occurred with the refractory ceramics at the lower test range. The metals likewise showed little reaction at their lower test temperatures.
nasa-tm-19700026628-conformal-coatings-f:
J. M. Fisher Jr. and C. J. Bryan of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida wrote this paper on protective coatings for printed wiring boards. A conformal coating is a thin skin that follows the shape of the board. It guards the circuits printed on it.

Such coatings have long served for moisture and corrosion protection, the authors note. They also insulate the board and make it tougher. The materials used range from epoxies and silicones to polyesters and polyurethanes. Kennedy's needs are special, they state, because the center sits on Florida's east coast. Its gear faces a wide mix of harsh weather and salt air.
podcast-dannyjones-RqtaH7kGIBo:
Historian Stephen Kinzer wrote the definitive popular history of MK-Ultra and its central figure, Sidney Gottlieb. He joins Danny Jones to tell that story in full. It is the CIA's secret quest for mind control, from its Cold War birth through LSD experiments on unwitting Americans. It ends with the destruction of the program's own records.

Kinzer's account is documented history, which sets this episode apart in the series: the strangest claims here carry footnotes. He follows Gottlieb from the program's founding to its exposure and explains why the agency pursued a goal its own scientists doubted. Jones mostly listens, and wisely. Listeners get the real MK-Ultra, stranger than its legend in the particulars, from the journalist who assembled it. Every other mind-control episode in this archive is best judged after this one.
podcast-joerogan-P038Pd440bo:
Comic Tom Segura joins Joe Rogan for episode 2429 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Segura co-hosts the hit Your Mom's House podcast and sells out arenas with his dry, dark stand-up. His Rogan visits feel like two comedy kings trading shop talk.

Segura shares stories from the road, from fatherhood, and from the odd fans who find him. He and Rogan compare notes on fame, hecklers, and the business of jokes. The laughs come easy, with the laid-back cruelty Segura's fans love. Loyal listeners get Your Mom's House energy on Rogan's turf.
podcast-tuckercarlson-zaFNktRoTbo:
Country singer John Rich returns to Tucker Carlson for a talk on Donald Trump, the dark tone of Eminem's new album, and a song Rich says God gave him. Rich is a star who mixes faith, fame, and plain talk. Carlson hosts the chat.

Rich tells what he makes of Trump now and why a rap star's dark work caught his ear. He tells how the song came to him, as he tells it, in a rush of grace. Carlson draws out the faith that runs through it all. Listeners get a star off stage and at ease. The library keeps the talk as a record of their chat.
the-paradise-of-children-from-a-wonder-b:
Nathaniel Hawthorne retold the story of Pandora as The Paradise of Children, one tale from A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys. The frame opens in the Tanglewood play-room at Christmas. Eustace Bright has come home from college, and a mighty snowstorm has shut the children in, with drifts so thick that even nearby trees vanish from the windows.

The contents promise the tale itself, framed by play-room scenes before and after. The children tumble in the snow, then gather indoors among their playthings, where a rocking-horse like a real pony stands biggest. Hawthorne uses the cozy, stormbound room to lead young listeners into the Greek myth.
the-siege-of-kimberley-its-humorous-and-: T. Phelan wrote The Siege of Kimberley, subtitled Its Humorous and Social Side. M. H. Gill and Son of Dublin published it in 1913. The siege belongs to the Anglo-Boer War of 1899 to 1902, the title says. Eighteen weeks are covered in eighteen chapters, it promises. The pages shown give the title and the contents only. Each chapter is named for the week it ends. The first ends on October 21, 1899. Weekly chapters then run through November and into December. The list shown stops at chapter eleven. No narrative text appears here.
the-vedanta-sutras-with-the-commentary-b: Part three of the Vedânta-Sûtras with the commentary by Râmânuja appeared in 1904 as volume forty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. George Thibaut translated the commentary into English. The material present here is the title page and a skeleton contents, so the sûtras and commentary themselves do not appear. Headings show an introduction followed by four chapters, called adhyâyas, each divided into four pâdas, or quarters. Only the first two chapters' divisions are listed before the pages end.
